name: domain-event
intent: Represent something that has happened in the domain as an immutable, past-tense event object, so the model can publish the fact and other parts of the model react to it while the publisher stays unaware of who reacts.
problem: A significant state change has to trigger reactions - updating another aggregate, notifying someone, recording history - and the reaction logic sits inline in the operation that caused the change. The rule is implicit, every new caller must remember it, and the code that changes state is coupled to everything that follows from the change.
context: An in-process domain model within one bounded context, where occurrences must be observable by more than one part of the model, where reactions change over time or belong to other subsystems, and where the aggregate that owns the state change must not depend on the reactions. It applies while the reactions live in the same process and can share or follow the publisher's transaction; a fact that must cross a process or context boundary is translated into an integration event instead.
benefits: Domain rules become explicit and named: a reaction that was hidden inside a service method turns into an event (OrderPlaced) plus handlers whose names state the rules they implement.
The publisher decouples from its consequences: the aggregate states a fact and does not know which handlers exist, so reactions are added by registration rather than by editing the model.

Aggregates stay small: one aggregate per transaction plus events for the rest gives eventual consistency across aggregate boundaries instead of one large, lock-heavy transaction (Vernon's fourth aggregate rule).
Events double as history: past-tense names, occurred-on timestamps and the collected event list give an audit trail, feed projections, and are the input format of event sourcing.
Reactions become independently testable: an event is a plain value, so a handler is tested by constructing the event and calling it - no model fixture and no running bus required.
Cross-cutting concerns (notifications, projections, analytics, cache invalidation) attach to the fact without touching the model that raises it.
tradeoffs: Indirection: the consequences of an operation are no longer visible at the call site, so understanding a state change means finding its subscribers - debugging and navigation get harder.

Consistency window: once reactions run in their own transactions the model is eventually consistent and there is no rollback across handlers; choosing in-transaction dispatch instead couples every handler failure into the publisher's transaction.

Delivery semantics: publishing after commit can lose events (the dual-write gap) unless dispatch is tied to the transaction or an outbox, while asynchronous dispatch delivers at least once and possibly out of order, so handlers must be idempotent and order-tolerant.
Event schemas become a contract: handlers, projections and other teams depend on event names and fields, so renaming or reshaping an event is a breaking change to the model's public surface.
Failure visibility: handler exceptions are either rolled into the publisher's transaction or swallowed by an error policy, and silent divergence between model and projections is hard to notice.
Over-abstraction: turning every trivial update into an event multiplies types and handlers faster than the domain grows, and each one is another place a rule can hide.

participants.responsibility: Immutable, past-tense representation of something that happened: carries the identity of the subject, the occurred-on time and exactly the data subscribers need - never references into the aggregate's live object graph.
Detects the significant state transition and constructs the event at that moment, collecting it rather than dispatching it; decides nothing about who reacts.
Reacts to one event type by updating a projection, notifying an external system or commanding another aggregate; owns its transaction and must tolerate redelivery and reordering.
Maintains the event-type to handler mapping and invokes the handlers; defines the timing semantics (synchronous or asynchronous, before or after commit) and the error policy.
Optional participant that appends events in occurrence order so history can be audited or replayed; with event sourcing the events are the authoritative state.
Optional participant at a bounded-context edge: converts a domain event into an integration event with a published schema for consumers in other services.
Captures events that failed all processing attempts; must be actively monitored to catch silent failures in the event pipeline.
Optional central registry (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS EventBridge Schema Discovery) that validates event schemas at publish time and enforces compatibility guarantees for consumers.

use_cases: Order lifecycle: placing an order raises OrderPlaced so stock is reserved, the buyer aggregate is validated or created, and a confirmation notification goes out — each reaction in its own handler.

Aggregate-to-aggregate consistency: committing a backlog item raises BacklogItemCommitted so the sprint records the commitment, keeping one aggregate per transaction and eventual consistency across the boundary (Vernon's example).
Accounting: a usage event is dispatched to posting rules that create accounting entries, turning tariff logic into named, replaceable handlers — well-suited to the Agreement Dispatcher pattern.

Audit and history: every state transition appends an event persisted with the aggregate, giving an audit log and — with event sourcing — a replayable history, point-in-time reconstruction, and retroactive projections.
In-process side effects after commit: cache invalidation, projector updates, search indexing and e-mail dispatch are wired as subscribers instead of inline calls.
CQRS read-model maintenance: the write model's committed events feed projectors that materialise read stores (Elasticsearch, Redis, denormalised tables); rebuilt by replaying the event log.

Cross-bounded-context integration: a domain event is translated at the boundary into an integration event with its own schema, published through a transactional outbox and consumed by other services via a message broker.

Saga/process manager coordination: a long-running workflow listens for events and sends commands in response, using the observed events as the record of progress rather than embedding workflow state in the aggregate.

Event streaming pipelines: domain events feed into Kafka, Pulsar, or Kinesis streams for downstream processing (analytics, ML feature stores, audit warehouses) while maintaining the event log as the source of truth.
Multi-tenant SaaS event isolation: events carry tenant identifiers and are partitioned by tenant ID so reactions are tenant-scoped and cross-tenant interference is prevented.
Feature flag and configuration propagation: domain events trigger evaluation of feature rules, dynamic configuration refresh, or A/B experiment allocation without polling.

Real-time monitoring and alerting: domain events feed into observability pipelines that detect business-level anomalies (unusual order volumes, compliance-triggering events) before they become operational incidents.
Event-driven microservices choreography: services emit domain events and react to each other's events without a central orchestrator, maintaining eventual consistency across service boundaries.

NestJS @nestjs/cqrs: an aggregate extends AggregateRoot (or implements IAggregateRoot via EventPublisher.mergeObjectContext) and raises events through apply(); the framework's EventPublisher drains the collected events onto the EventBus at the dispatch point, and @EventsHandler classes react - the raise-collect-dispatch flow made concrete.

Spring Modulith: modules communicate by publishing domain events with Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher instead of holding cross-module bean dependencies; @ApplicationModuleListener declares the receiving side and the Event Publication Registry records each publication transactionally so incomplete deliveries can be resubmitted.

Axon Framework: aggregates publish through AggregateLifecycle.apply(...), which stamps the event with the aggregate identifier and sequence number, appends it for event-sourced state, and then dispatches it on the EventBus - non-aggregate code publishes via EventGateway.
avoid_when: The reaction is part of the same invariant: call the collaborator or a domain service directly; an explicit call inside the transaction expresses atomicity better than a bus.
There is exactly one permanent listener and no expectation of more (for example one log line): a direct call or an audit interceptor is simpler and easier to debug.
The consumer lives in another process or bounded context: publish an integration event through a broker (messaging gateway, event message) and keep the domain event for in-process reactions.
You need the current state rather than the occurrence: query the repository or the read model instead of replaying events.
The requirement is a long-running, multi-step workflow with waits and compensation: model it with a process manager rather than by chaining domain events.
anti_patterns: CRUD events: raising UserUpdated or OrderChanged for every field write, forcing every handler to diff payloads to learn what happened; events must be business-significant occurrences.
Fat events that embed the aggregate's entire state: the meaning of the event becomes unclear and every consumer is coupled to the model's internals.
Using the in-process bus as a message broker: publishing domain events across processes or contexts and calling that an integration architecture.
Events as hidden hooks for invariants that must hold atomically: the rule is enforced by a subscriber found only at runtime instead of inside the transaction that must keep it true.
Publishing after the commit and calling it reliable without an outbox: the classic dual-write gap, where a crash between commit and publish silently drops the event.

Storing value objects inside domain events: value objects may reject invalid arguments based on current validation rules, which can prevent deserialization of historical events when those rules change; use flat scalar fields instead.

Skipping sequence numbers on high-throughput aggregates: without them, detecting missed or duplicate events requires expensive global-position tracking; sequence numbers make idempotency checks trivial.

Infinite event loops: A→B→C→A cycles where each service reacts to the previous one's events without a cycle-breaking mechanism; model cyclic dependencies with a process manager or explicit workflow state.

Silent swallowing of handler errors: using broad try-catch that silently continues rather than routing failures to a dead-letter queue; silent divergence between publisher state and projections goes undetected.
Mixing domain events with integration events: using the same event type for in-process handlers and cross-service communication, so internal refactoring breaks external consumers.
design_principles: Ubiquitous language: event names are past-tense domain facts, not technical notifications.
Inversion of control: the publisher depends on an abstract dispatch port; subscribers depend on the event, never on the publisher.
Single responsibility: the aggregate owns the state transition, handlers own the side effects, the dispatcher owns the routing.
Open/closed principle: new reactions are new handlers registered at the edge; the model that raises the events stays closed for modification.
Encapsulation: events expose identities and minimal data, so handlers cannot reach into or mutate the aggregate.
Consistency-boundary discipline: one aggregate mutated per transaction, with eventual consistency through events across aggregate boundaries.
Envelope pattern: wrap event payloads in an envelope with mandatory metadata (event ID, type, version, timestamp, source) to support schema evolution and routing without modifying the payload schema.
Per-aggregate ordering: events for the same aggregate must be processed in order; global ordering across aggregates is rarely needed and needlessly limits throughput.
Idempotent by design: handlers are designed to safely process the same event more than once, not merely documented as idempotent.
best_practices: Name events for what happened (past tense, ubiquitous language) and include occurred-on plus the identifiers subscribers need; treat each event schema as a permanent, versioned contract.
Raise the event inside the aggregate at the transition, collect it on the aggregate or unit of work, and dispatch once at an explicit boundary instead of scattering publish calls.
Prefer dispatch after commit for side effects; when a reaction must be transactional, dispatch before commit and accept that handler failure rolls back the change.

Persist the event and the state change in the same transaction using an outbox table (transactional outbox pattern): write business data and outbox row atomically, then relay to the broker from the outbox — never as a second independent write.
Make handlers idempotent (track processed event IDs) and order-tolerant; keep each one small and give it its own transaction unless atomicity with the publisher is genuinely required.
Keep the in-process subscriber list short and translate to an integration event with its own contract for anything outside the model; external systems should not subscribe to domain events directly.
Test handlers as functions of an event, and assert the aggregate's raised-event list separately from the dispatch wiring.

Version event schemas additively (add optional fields); use upcasting (pure function that transforms old payload to current shape at read time) for non-additive changes; never delete an old event type's deserializer while unprocessed instances exist in the store.

Use sequence numbers (monotonically increasing per aggregate) to detect gaps, enable optimistic concurrency control, and support point-in-time reconstruction; expose them in integration events for downstream consumers.
For long-lived aggregates, take snapshots every N events; version the snapshot schema and fall back to full replay when the stored snapshot version is older than the code expects.

Cross-process consumers must receive integration events, not raw domain events; the Integration-Event Translator converts domain events at the bounded-context boundary with a published schema and its own compatibility guarantees.
Partition events by aggregate ID (e.g., Kafka partition key, SQS FIFO message group ID) to guarantee per-aggregate ordering while scaling handlers horizontally across partitions.
Implement retry budgets per handler: after N retries, route to a dead-letter queue rather than retrying indefinitely and blocking the pipeline; monitor DLQ depth and age actively.
Use an event envelope (event ID, correlation ID, causation ID, schema version) to support distributed tracing across event chains and enable routing without payload changes.
Apply consumer-driven contract testing for integration events: consumers publish their expected schema, the registry enforces compatibility before publishers can publish breaking changes.

For high-throughput systems, enrich events lazily (on first read after a schema change) rather than rewriting history; use lazy enrichment (write a new event to the stream) only when enrichment data cannot be derived from existing fields.
Monitor event processing latency (P50/P95/P99), retry rates per handler, dead-letter queue depth, and ordering violation counts as first-class production metrics.
Validate event schemas against a schema registry at publish time (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS EventBridge Schema Discovery) to catch breaking changes before they reach consumers.
